va_froopy_land_pillar.blurb: A large freestanding pillar propped against the cliff at Pinnacle Rock, on the Virginia side of Breaks Interstate Park in the far southwest of the state. It holds a dozen routes: eight bolted sport lines and four trad climbs. Grades start around 5.7 and 5.8, but most of the climbing sits in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, so it suits climbers comfortable on the middle to upper grades rather than beginners. The pillar forms a narrow passage alongside the main wall, and the cliff section next to it adds a further group of routes in the same sector.

va_big_schloss.blurb: A small ridge-top crag on Great North Mountain in the George Washington National Forest, along the Virginia and West Virginia line. The climbing is on a band of white sandstone roughly 45 to 60 feet tall near the crest, with a handful of trad and top-rope lines from 5.4 up to about 5.8. Scattered boulders along the ridge add problems from very easy up to V3, though most are mellow. Rock quality varies, with lichen and loose blocks reported in places, and little traffic means you should expect to test holds and do some cleaning. It is a quiet, scenic spot rather than a destination crag.

va_crooked_road_boulder.blurb: A single tall, dark and steep boulder in the Boneyard boulderfield at Grayson Highlands State Park in southwest Virginia, with a committing highball feel. It carries about a dozen problems that run from the easiest grades up to V7, with an even spread through V2 to V5 and a couple of harder lines at the top end. Boneyard boulders sit well apart on the mountainside, so the area tends to feel uncrowded even on busy days. A good stop for climbers who like bigger, more serious problems.
